body: ### Describe the feature you want to add to this project This enhancement introduces: ✅ ADF-based stationarity testing ✅ Trend, ACF, and seasonal decomposition plots ✅ Support for both pandas.Series and DataFrame inputs ✅ Optional Plotly interactive visualization mode ✅ A complete, headless-safe test suite ### Describe your proposed solution I propose adding a comprehensive Time-Series EDA module that allows users to analyze series properties with a single function call. Based on my exploration, this module should include: * Stationarity Testing: Integration of ADF (Augmented Dickey-Fuller) tests to check for unit roots. * Decomposition: Visualizing Trend, Seasonality, and Residuals (using seasonal_decompose). * Correlation Plots: Auto-Correlation Function (ACF) plots to identify lag significance. * Flexibility: Support for both pandas.Series and DataFrame inputs. * Interactivity: An option to switch between static (Matplotlib) and interactive (Plotly) visualization modes. ### Describe alternatives you've considered, if relevant Users currently have to manually import statsmodels or scipy to perform these checks separately, which breaks the low-code philosophy of PyCaret. ### Additional context I have already drafted a solution for this. I focused on designing modular APIs and ensuring the test suite is headless-safe for CI/CD environments. I am submitting a PR for this feature here: #4171
title: [Feature Request] Implementation of Time-Series Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA) Module

body:
### pycaret version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported [here](https://github.com/pycaret/pycaret/issues).

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://github.com/pycaret/pycaret/releases) of pycaret.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the master branch of pycaret (pip install -U git+https://github.com/pycaret/pycaret.git@master).


### Issue Description

Running compare_models with 'lightgbm' works 50 times slower than expected. The root cause of this is busy waiting in libgomp library used by 'lightgbm'. It is doing this busy waiting synchronization when 'n_jobs' is unset/default. This issue is avoided when n_jobs is set to 1. 

### Reproducible Example

```python
# ---
# jupyter:
#   jupytext:
#     text_representation:
#       extension: .py
#       format_name: light
#       format_version: '1.5'
#       jupytext_version: 1.16.4
#   kernelspec:
#     display_name: Python 3 (ipykernel)
#     language: python
#     name: python3
# ---

# +
import pandas as pd
import random

random.seed(42)

num_rows = 1024
ids = [i for i in range(num_rows)]
fav = [i % 3 for i in range(num_rows)]
age = [20 + random.randrange(60) for i in range(num_rows)]


def transform(age, fav):
    if age > 50 and age < 70 and fav == 1:
        return 1
    else:
        return 0


buy = [transform(age[i], fav[i]) for i in range(num_rows)]

df = pd.DataFrame({"ids": ids, "fav": fav, "age": age, "buy": buy})

from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

df_train, df_test = train_test_split(df, test_size=0.33)

print(df_train.shape)
print(df_test.shape)

# +
from contextlib import contextmanager
from timeit import default_timer


@contextmanager
def elapsed_timer():
    start = default_timer()
    elapser = lambda: default_timer() - start
    yield lambda: elapser()
    end = default_timer()
    elapser = lambda: end - start


# +
from pycaret.classification import ClassificationExperiment
from sklearn.model_selection import KFold
from lightgbm.sklearn import LGBMClassifier

fold_strategy = KFold(n_splits=3, shuffle=True, random_state=49)

experiment = ClassificationExperiment()
experiment.setup(
    data=df_train[["fav", "age", "buy"]],
    test_data=df_test[["fav", "age", "buy"]],
    target="buy",
    fold_strategy=fold_strategy,
    data_split_shuffle=False,
    numeric_features=["age"],
    categorical_features=["fav"],
    normalize=True,
    session_id=1234,
)

with elapsed_timer() as elapsed:
    models = experiment.compare_models(
        include=[LGBMClassifier(n_jobs=1)],  ### FAST - it takes 2 seconds
        sort="AUC",
        n_select=1,
    )
    print(f"{elapsed()=}")

with elapsed_timer() as elapsed:
    models = experiment.compare_models(
        include=["lightgbm"], sort="AUC", n_select=1  ### SLOW - it takes 50 seconds
    )
    print(f"{elapsed()=}")
# -
```

### Expected Behavior

It is expected that execution with 'n_jobs unset' works comparable or faster then execution with 'n_jobs=1'.

```python-traceback
n_jobs unset elapsed()=52.359305076002784
```

In your code

you've specified all features (including numeric ones like age, family_size, and work_experience) as categorical. This causes PyCaret to apply one-hot encoding to all of them.

Why This Is Problematic:
- Columns like age often contain many unique values (e.g., each person might have a different age). One-hot encoding will create one binary column per unique age.
- Applying one-hot encoding to such features results in one binary column per unique value, leading to:
High-dimensional sparse matrices
Increased memory usage
Risk of overfitting
Poor model generalization

✅ Recommendation:
Treat age, family_size, and work_experience as numeric features, not categorical. If you still want to treat them categorically (e.g., to represent age groups), consider binning first.
Update your setup() like this:
`s = setup(
    data=df.drop('target', axis=1),
    target='target',
    categorical_features=['gender', 'ever_married', 'graduated', 'profession', 'spending_score'],
    session_id=123
)
`

This ensures:
- Only true categorical features are encoded.
- Numerical features are handled correctly by scaling or imputation.

body:
### In compare and create results of classification.

Currently, PyCaret shows a weighted average for model performance, but this doesn't always tell the full story. For example, if you have two classes like "yes" and "no," and the model performs really well for "no" but poorly for "yes," the weighted score might still look good. This can hide the fact that the model isn't doing well on the minority class ("yes").

The problem is, you might end up selecting and deploying the model that looks the best based on these weighted scores, but in reality, it’s the worst model for catching the minority class. What you really need is to focus on metrics that show the performance of each class, especially the minority ones, so you can truly understand how well the model is working for all your data.



### Describe your proposed solution

Best will be to show results of all classes which is like shown in classification report of sklearn.

### Describe alternatives you've considered, if relevant

_No response_

### Additional context

_No response_

- [X] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported [here](https://github.com/pycaret/pycaret/issues).

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the master branch of pycaret (pip install -U git+https://github.com/pycaret/pycaret.git@master).


### Issue Description

When using the setup function with the feature_selection=True parameter in Pycaret 3.3.2, this error is returned.
"ValueError: The feature names should match those that were passed during fit."

### Reproducible Example

```python
## At the Anaconda command line, run the following commands
conda create -n pycaret_332_310_2 python=3.10
# Press y when prompted
conda activate pycaret_332_310_2
pip install pycaret[full] ipykernel
python -m ipykernel install --user --name=pycaret_332_310_2
jupyter notebook

## Then open a new notebook, select the pycaret_332_310_2 kernel and run the following code.
from pycaret.datasets import get_data
data = get_data('diabetes')

from pycaret.classification import *
s = setup(data, target = 'Class variable', session_id = 123,
         feature_selection=True)
```


### Expected Behavior

I expect the code to return a data table and a successful setup screen, which is what I get when I omit the feature_selection=True parameter.

title: [BUG]: Feature selection in pycaret.classification setup function error

body:
### pycaret version checks

- [X] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported [here](https://github.com/pycaret/pycaret/issues).

- [X] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://github.com/pycaret/pycaret/releases) of pycaret.

- [X] I have confirmed this bug exists on the master branch of pycaret (pip install -U git+https://github.com/pycaret/pycaret.git@master).


### Issue Description

The setup function in PyCaret's ClassificationExperiment is failing when trying to process categorical variables during data preprocessing. The error occurs specifically when attempting to impute missing values in categorical columns using the iterative imputer.

### Reproducible Example

```python
# Perform stratified cross-validation for the
skf = StratifiedKFold(n_splits=cv, shuffle=True, random_state=42)
  
for fold, (idx_train, idx_test) in enumerate(skf.split(data_df, data_df[label_name])):

    # Get the training and test data if not independent test was given
    test_df = data_df.iloc[idx_test] if test_df is None else test_df

    # Initialize  and Set up the classification experiment Object
    clf_exp = ClassificationExperiment()
    clf_exp.setup(data=data_df.iloc[idx_train], target=label_name, test_data=data_df.iloc[idx_test],  **exp_params)
exp_params = { exp_name: f'classification-exp-{fold}'
 'train_size': 0.8,
 'numeric_imputation': 'knn',
 'categorical_imputation': 'mode',
 'imputation_type': 'iterative',

 'fix_imbalance': True,

 'transformation': False,
```

### Expected Behavior

The setup function should successfully preprocess the data, including imputing missing values in categorical columns using the iterative imputer. if I ommit the test_data in the experiment setup and then use the function         preds = clf_exp.predict_model(best_model, data=test_df) works perfectly. the limitation is in that case is that i am not able to fully set my train test to 1.0 (whole dataset).

### Issue Description

## [Bug]: `blend_models()` and `stack_models()` Fail with Certain Models Above 1000 Samples

**Description:**

This issue appears to be related to a problem with PyCaret's `blend_models()` and `stack_models()` functions when using certain models and exceeding 1000 samples. The error occurs during the finalization stage of model creation, resulting in a "ValueError: cannot set WRITEABLE flag to True of this array" error. This issue does not appear to be related to memory limitations, as testing on systems with 8-24 cores and 32-128 GB of RAM did not solve the problem. 

**Reproducible Code:**
I've included a reproducible example below.

**Affected Models:**

The following models cause the error when included in `blend_models()` or `stack_models()`:

* `lda`, `ridge`, `ada`, `dt`, `gbc`, `nb`, `et`, `rf`, `qda`

All other models tested (including `svm`, `lr`, `xgboost`, `lightgbm`, `knn`, `catboost`, and `dummy`) work without issue when combined.  Furthermore, blending or stacking using a single `dt` model also causes the error. This indicates the issue is likely related to how PyCaret handles models like these during the finalization step.

**Observations:**

* **Finalization Error:** The error appears when PyCaret is "Finalizing Model" during the blending or stacking process.
* **Manual Ensemble Success:** Manually creating and fitting ensembles (using `VotingClassifier` and `StackingClassifier`) does not produce this error.
* **Dataset Size:**  The error only occurs when the dataset size exceeds 1000 rows.
* **Memory Profiler:**  Memory profiling (using `memory_profiler`) indicates that the memory usage remains below 400 MB, for both 500 and 750 samples with on a 4-5 MB increase, suggesting that the problem is not memory-related.
* **Versions:**  The issue persists across PyCaret versions (including master branch) and `scikit-learn` versions 1.4.1 and above. 
* **Data Writability:**  The DataFrame is writable at all stages, before and after setup, model creation, and even after the error occurs.

**References:**

* [Chinese Blog Mentioning Similar Issue](https://qiita.com/maskot1977/items/a3730bbc4ade41ade7e1) 

**Request:**

This issue appears to be a bug in PyCaret's `blend_models()` and `stack_models()` functions. Any assistance in resolving this would be greatly appreciated. 

**Additional Context:** 

* The error occurs even with a dataset of just 1000 rows, which is relatively small.
* The issue appears to be related to the way PyCaret handles specific models during the finalization process of blending or stacking. 
* The problem persists across various versions of PyCaret and `scikit-learn`.


### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
from pycaret.classification import ClassificationExperiment

# Generate Synthetic Data
train_data = pd.DataFrame(np.random.rand(750, 384))  # Works for 750 or less
# train_data = pd.DataFrame(np.random.rand(5000, 384))  # Fails for 1000 or more
train_data['target'] = np.random.randint(0, 2, len(train_data))

# Ensure a copy is made
train_data = train_data.copy(deep=True) 

# Check Data Writability
print(f"DataFrame Flags Before Setup: {train_data.values.flags}")

exp = ClassificationExperiment()
exp.setup(data=train_data, target='target', session_id=123, fold=3, verbose=True)

print(f"DataFrame Flags After Setup: {train_data.values.flags}")

# Create Models
lr = exp.create_model('lr')
dt = exp.create_model('dt')
knn = exp.create_model('knn')

print(f"DataFrame Flags After Creating Models: {train_data.values.flags}")

# Attempt to blend models (this is where the error likely occurs)
try:
    blended_model = exp.blend_models(estimator_list=[lr, dt, knn])
    
    # Check DataFrame flags after blending
    print(f"DataFrame Flags After Blending: {train_data.values.flags}")
except ValueError as e:
    print(f"Error: {e}")
    print(f"DataFrame Flags After Blending Error: {train_data.values.flags}")

# Attempt to stack models (this is where the error likely occurs)
try:
    stacked_model = exp.stack_models(estimator_list=[lr, dt, knn], meta_model=LogisticRegression())
    
    # Check DataFrame flags after stacking
    print(f"DataFrame Flags After Stacking: {train_data.values.flags}")
except ValueError as e:
    print(f"Error: {e}")
    print(f"DataFrame Flags After Stacking Error: {train_data.values.flags}")

# --- (Optional: Manually create and fit models to show no issue) --- 
voting_clf = VotingClassifier(
    estimators=[('lr', lr), ('dt', dt), ('knn', knn)], 
    voting='hard' 
)
voting_clf.fit(train_data.drop('target', axis=1), train_data['target'])

estimators = [
    ('lr', lr),

]
stacked_clf = StackingClassifier(
    estimators=estimators, 
    final_estimator=LogisticRegression()
)
stacked_clf.fit(train_data.drop('target', axis=1), train_data['target'])
```

title: [BUG]: not all models compared in `compare_models`

body:
### pycaret version checks

- [X] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported [here](https://github.com/pycaret/pycaret/issues).

- [X] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://github.com/pycaret/pycaret/releases) of pycaret.

- [X] I have confirmed this bug exists on the master branch of pycaret (pip install -U git+https://github.com/pycaret/pycaret.git@master).


### Issue Description

when columns with datetime dtype have nulls during training, pycaret does not create the features `column_day`, `column_month`, `column_year`, however during inference, if the used data does not have any nulls in those same date columns, then pycaret creates those columns leading to this error

```python
ValueError: The feature names should match those that were passed during fit.
Feature names unseen at fit time:
- policies_inception_date_day
- policies_inception_date_month
- policies_inception_date_year
- policies_sold_date_day
- policies_sold_date_month
```

the columns `policies_sold` and `policies_inception` have missing values in training data but not in inference data.

the model used is a random forest which as far as I know does not handle missing values but still training completes with no issues.

this error occurred in production, when attempting to reproduce with a synthetic dataset I get a different error during setup but it is basically the same, also about date features transformation

```python
KeyError: "['start_date_year', 'start_date_month', 'start_date_day'] not in index"
```

I set some of the values in `start_date` column to None on purpose to reproduce the ValueError but ran into this error instead, it seems like pycaret is expecting those features to exist when they were not created because there are missing values in that column

### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd
import random
import numpy as np
from pycaret.classification import ClassificationExperiment
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

# create synthetic data with multiple columns including a datetime column
np.random.seed(0)
n = 1000
df = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "start_date": pd.date_range(start="1/1/2020", periods=n, freq="H"),
        "end_date": pd.date_range(start="1/1/2020", periods=n, freq="H")
        + pd.Timedelta(hours=1),
        "cat1": np.random.choice(["A", "B", "C"], n),
        "A": np.random.rand(n),
        "B": np.random.rand(n),
        "C": np.random.rand(n),
        "D": np.random.rand(n),
        "E": np.random.rand(n),
        "F": np.random.rand(n),
        "G": np.random.rand(n),
        "target": np.random.randint(0, 2, n),
    }
)

train, test = train_test_split(df, test_size=0.2, random_state=0)
train.reset_index(drop=True, inplace=True)
test.reset_index(drop=True, inplace=True)


# set 10% of dates to be missing
n_missing = int(0.1 * len(train))
missing_idx = random.sample(range(len(train)), n_missing)
train.loc[missing_idx, "start_date"] = np.nan


exp = ClassificationExperiment()

attr_dict = {
    "target": "target",
    "verbose": True,
    "memory": False,
    "log_experiment": True,
    "remove_multicollinearity": True,
    "imputation_type": None,
    "remove_outliers": False,
    "multicollinearity_threshold": 0.6,
    "fold": 5,
}

exp.setup(data=train, **attr_dict) # this fails with KeyError
```


### Expected Behavior

- pycaret will not split date columns to individual components during inference if that was not done during training.
- pycaret will not raise a KeyError about date column components if they were not created.

### pycaret version checks

- [X] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported [here](https://github.com/pycaret/pycaret/issues).

- [X] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://github.com/pycaret/pycaret/releases) of pycaret.

- [X] I have confirmed this bug exists on the master branch of pycaret (pip install -U git+https://github.com/pycaret/pycaret.git@master).

### Issue Description

When using PyCaret's clustering module with large datasets, particularly those exceeding 1 million rows, users face significant challenges due to the mandatory calculation of certain evaluation metrics, such as the silhouette score. The lack of flexibility in disabling or customizing these metrics during the `setup()` function is a critical issue. The silhouette score's computational complexity is O(n^2), making its evaluation impractical for large datasets due to the excessive time and computational resources required.

The primary concern is not with the calculation method of the silhouette score but with the compulsory nature of its evaluation. This automatic evaluation can render clustering operations infeasible on large datasets, as users currently do not have the option to omit this expensive metric calculation.

### Proposed Enhancements

To resolve this, I propose enhancing the `setup()` function to allow users to specify which evaluation metrics should be calculated, similar to how they can currently choose which algorithms to train. This could be achieved by introducing a parameter such as `include_metrics` or `exclude_metrics`, offering flexibility in metric computation. For instance:

```python
from pycaret.clustering import setup
setup(data, include_metrics=['sse', 'dbscan'], exclude_metrics=['silhouette'])`)
```

This approach would allow users to tailor the computational load according to their dataset size and the specific requirements of their analysis, thereby enabling efficient clustering of very large datasets.

### Benefits of the Enhancement

Implementing this feature would:

- Make PyCaret's clustering module scalable and more adaptable to large-scale data environments.
- Reduce computational costs and execution times, making it feasible to cluster large datasets.
- Increase user control over the analytical process, enhancing PyCaret’s utility in diverse applications.

Thank you for considering this enhancement, also please let me know if you think this is a great addition and give advice where changes should be implemented. Happy to raise the PR.


### Reproducible Example

```python
I conducted benchmark tests comparing model training times and memory usage between plain scikit-learn KMeans and PyCaret's setup, specifically focusing on the impact of automatic silhouette score calculations in large datasets. The script includes detailed logging and measurement of memory consumption and processing times for datasets ranging from 1 to 4 million rows.

Findings clearly show that the exponential increase in computation time and memory usage in PyCaret setups is primarily due to the evaluation of the silhouette score, not from the training process itself. The benchmarking script provided insights into how the inclusion of this metric significantly impacts the feasibility of clustering operations in large-scale settings.


import logging

# Set the logging level to DEBUG
logging.basicConfig(level=logging.DEBUG)

import time

import mlflow

mlflow.autolog(disable=True)

import pandas as pd
import plotly.express as px
import seaborn as sns
from memory_profiler import memory_usage
from pycaret.clustering import ClusteringExperiment, create_model, setup
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import LabelEncoder

# Could be related to https://github.com/pycaret/pycaret/issues/3371?


def widen_dataset(df, num_columns):
    # Get the number of columns in the original dataset
    original_num_columns = df.shape[1]

    # Calculate the number of times the columns need to be repeated
    repeat_times = num_columns // original_num_columns

    # Repeat the columns and add a suffix to each column name
    df_repeated = pd.concat(
        [df.add_suffix(f"_{i}") for i in range(repeat_times)], axis=1
    )

    # If there are still columns needed, add them from the beginning of the dataframe
    remaining_columns = num_columns % original_num_columns
    if remaining_columns > 0:
        df_remaining = df[df.columns[:remaining_columns]].add_suffix(f"_{repeat_times}")
        df_repeated = pd.concat([df_repeated, df_remaining], axis=1)

    return df_repeated


def lengthen_dataset(df, num_rows):
    # Repeat the dataset until we reach the desired number of rows
    while len(df) < num_rows:
        df = pd.concat([df, df])

    # Trim the dataset to exactly the desired number of rows
    df = df.iloc[:num_rows]

    # Reset the index of the DataFrame
    df = df.reset_index(drop=True)

    return df


def fit_kmeans(df):
    # Initialize a KMeans model with 4 clusters
    kmeans = KMeans(n_clusters=4)

    # Fit the model to the dataset
    kmeans.fit(df)


def plot_memory_consumption(df):
    # Melt the DataFrame to a long format
    df_melted = df.melt(
        id_vars="Number of Rows",
        var_name="Process",
        value_name="Memory Consumption (MiB)",
    )

    # Create the plot with Plotly Express
    fig = px.line(
        df_melted,
        x="Number of Rows",
        y="Memory Consumption (MiB)",
        color="Process",
        markers=True,
    )
    fig.show()


def plot_memory_consumption(df):
    # Melt the DataFrame to a long format
    df_melted = df.melt(
        id_vars=["Number of Rows", "Library"],
        var_name="Process",
        value_name="Value",
    )

    # Create the plot with Plotly Express
    fig = px.line(
        df_melted,
        x="Number of Rows",
        y="Value",
        color="Library",
        facet_row="Process",
        markers=True,
    )

    # Update facet titles
    fig.update_yaxes(title_text="Processing Time (s)", row=1, col=1)
    fig.update_yaxes(title_text="Memory Consumption (MiB)", row=2, col=1)

    # Set y-axes to scale automatically
    fig.update_yaxes(matches=None)

    # Save the plot as a high-quality PNG file
    fig.write_image("memory_consumption.png", scale=2)


def create_memory_df(row_numbers, model_memory, libraries, processing_times):
    # Create a DataFrame from the memory consumption data
    df = pd.DataFrame(
        {
            "Number of Rows": row_numbers,
            "Memory Consumption": model_memory,
            "Library": libraries,
            "Processing Time": processing_times,
        }
    )
    return df


def label_encode_columns(df, columns):
    # Initialize a label encoder
    le = LabelEncoder()

    # Loop over the list of columns
    for column in columns:
        # Check if the column exists in the DataFrame
        if column in df.columns:
            # Transform the column
            df[column] = le.fit_transform(df[column])

    return df


def get_mock_data(num_rows):
    # Load the iris dataset
    iris = sns.load_dataset("iris")

    # Widen the dataset
    iris_wide = widen_dataset(iris, 15)

    # Lengthen the dataset
    iris_long = lengthen_dataset(iris_wide, num_rows)

    # Label encode the 'species' columns
    iris_long = label_encode_columns(iris_long, ["species_0", "species_1", "species_2"])

    return iris_long

def fit_kmeans_pycaret(df):
    s = ClusteringExperiment()
    s.setup(
        data=df,
        verbose=False,
        normalize=False,
        index=False,
        transformation=False,
        pca=False,
        preprocess=False,
        remove_outliers=False,
        system_log=False,
        log_experiment=False,
        log_plots=False,
        log_profile=False,
        log_data=False,
        memory=False,
        profile=False,
    )

    kmeans = s.create_model(
        "kmeans",
        # verbose=False,
    )
    return kmeans

def collect_memory_data():
    # Initialize lists to store the memory consumption data
    model_memory = []
    row_numbers = []
    libraries = []
    processing_times = []

    # Start at 500,000 rows and increase by 500,000 each time
    for num_rows in range(1000000, 4000001, 100000):
        for library in ["scikit", "pycaret"]:
            # Get the mock data
            iris_long = get_mock_data(num_rows)

            # Define a function to call fit_kmeans with iris_long
            def fit_model():
                if library == "scikit":
                    return fit_kmeans(iris_long)
                elif library == "pycaret":
                    return fit_kmeans_pycaret(iris_long)

            # Capture peak memory usage and processing time during the fit_model call
            start_time = time.time()
            mem_usage_model = max(memory_usage(proc=fit_model))
            end_time = time.time()

            # Calculate processing time and add it to the list
            processing_time = end_time - start_time
            processing_times.append(processing_time)

            # Add the peak memory usage to the model_memory list
            model_memory.append(mem_usage_model)

            # Add the number of rows to the list
            row_numbers.append(num_rows)

            # Add the library to the list
            libraries.append(library)

            # Log the current step and parameters
            logging.info(
                f"Step completed. Rows: {num_rows}, Library: {library}, Model Memory: {mem_usage_model}, Processing Time: {processing_time}"
            )

    return row_numbers, model_memory, libraries, processing_times


if __name__ == "__main__":
    # Call the function to collect the memory consumption data
    row_numbers, dataset_memory, model_memory, libraries = collect_memory_data()

    # Call the function to create the DataFrame
    df = create_memory_df(row_numbers, dataset_memory, model_memory, libraries)

    # Call the plotting function
    plot_memory_consumption(df)
```

### Describe the feature you want to add to this project

In statistics and econometrics, a distributed lag model is a model for time series data in which a regression equation is used to predict current values of a dependent variable based on both the current values of an explanatory variable and the lagged (past period) values of this explanatory variable  .

The starting point for a distributed lag model is an assumed structure of the form:

\[ y_t = a + w_0x_t + w_1x_{t-1} + w_2x_{t-2} + \ldots + \text{error term} \]

or the form:

\[ y_t = a + w_0x_t + w_1x_{t-1} + w_2x_{t-2} + \ldots + w_nx_{t-n} + \text{error term} \]

where \(y_t\) is the value at time period \(t\) of the dependent variable \(y\), \(a\) is the intercept term to be estimated, and \(w_i\) is called the lag weight (also to be estimated) placed on the value \(i\) periods previously of the explanatory variable \(x\). In the first equation, the dependent variable is assumed to be affected by values of the independent variable arbitrarily far in the past, so the number of lag weights is infinite and the model is called an infinite distributed lag model. In the alternative, second, equation, there are only a finite number of lag weights, indicating an assumption that there is a maximum lag beyond which values of the independent variable do not affect the dependent variable; a model based on this assumption is called a finite distributed lag model.

In an infinite distributed lag model, an infinite number of lag weights need to be estimated; clearly this can be done only if some structure is assumed for the relation between the various lag weights, with the entire infinitude of them expressible in terms of a finite number of assumed underlying parameters. I found a workaround for this...
After checking the [source code](https://github.com/pycaret/pycaret/blob/885ebb81055ac017e50080db7731973d1a222e19/pycaret/internal/preprocess/transformers.py#L135), the error is caused by setting up a merge between the `original_df` and the transformed `df`, just so that they can merge. But due to oversampling with SMOTE on the minority class, the two indices do not align.

The main purpose for this class method is to return a `df` that has the correct ordering of the columns.
Order does not really matter in my case, and I have not checked any downstream implications of this fix...

If you care about ordering, you can add your own column order with monkey patch fix below at `...` .

```python
from pycaret.internal.preprocess.transformers import TransformerWrapper

def _reorder_cols(self, df, original_df):
  ...
  return df

TransformerWrapper._reorder_cols = _reorder_cols
```

I have the exact same problem. I investigated a little bit about the reason for this bug. Basically when the line is executed 
`model_results["model"] = model[0]`
The model column is created and inserted into the dataframe model_results. But when inserting into the dataframe pandas performs some checks on the type of object to be inserted inside the row.
In this specific case the type that is detected is a list_like in the section 
```python
if is_list_like(value):
          com.require_length_match(value, self.index)
```
`is_list_like` returns true since the model has the attribute  `__iter__ `and then goes into the if and tries to execute the `require_length_match` function. The problem is that the model does not have the `len` attribute and so the `require_length_match` function fails.
Is there a workaround to fix this bug?

> Is there a workaround to fix this bug?

Not within pycaret as far as I've found. The workaround I've used is to run the threshold optimization myself and create a wrapper class which uses the optimized threshold on calls to predict_model. To optimize the threshold, you can do a shgo optimization as is implemented in pycaret, but since the problem is just 1D, it's also simple enough to create a linspaced array and check which threshold optimizes your metric of interest. It would be nice however if this were resolved within pycaret. Especially when optimizing for a 0/1 loss like accuracy, where thresholding can dramatically change the model's performance, it should be done behind the scenes during the model_compare and tune_model steps.
@christopherkottke can you make a pull-request?
It appears that the error occurs only with certain models, specifically 'gbc', 'ada', 'et', 'catboost', and 'rf'
Has the error been resolved? It seems that the optimized threshold is not working with some tree models.

body:
### pycaret version checks

- [X] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported [here](https://github.com/pycaret/pycaret/issues).

- [X] I have confirmed this bug exists on the master branch of pycaret (pip install -U git+https://github.com/pycaret/pycaret.git@master).


### Issue Description

predict_model() prints wrong accuracy, precision, and recall score when target is of object dtype.

### Reproducible Example

```python


# +
# tutorial from https://nbviewer.org/github/pycaret/pycaret/blob/master/tutorials/Tutorial%20-%20Binary%20Classification.ipynb
# -

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

# +
from sklearn.metrics import accuracy_score, precision_score, recall_score, f1_score, cohen_kappa_score, matthews_corrcoef

def metrics_binary(y_true, y_pred, pos_label=1):
    return pd.DataFrame({'value':[accuracy_score(y_true, y_pred),
                                  precision_score(y_true, y_pred, pos_label=pos_label),
                                  recall_score(y_true, y_pred, pos_label=pos_label),
                                  f1_score(y_true, y_pred, pos_label=pos_label),
                                  cohen_kappa_score(y_true, y_pred),
                                  matthews_corrcoef(y_true, y_pred)]},
                         index = ['acc', 'precision', 'recall',
                                  'f1', 'kappa', 'mcc'])


# -

from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

# +


# loading sample dataset from pycaret dataset module
from pycaret.datasets import get_data
data = get_data('diabetes')


# -

data.columns



# ### target 0 or 1

X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(data.drop('Class variable', axis=1),
                                                    data['Class variable'],
                                                    test_size=0.2)



dat_train = pd.concat([X_train, y_train], axis=1)
dat_test = pd.concat([X_test, y_test], axis=1)

# +


# import pycaret classification and init setup
from pycaret.classification import *
s = setup(dat_train, target = 'Class variable', 
      test_data = dat_test,
          session_id = 123)


# -

gbc = s.create_model('gbc')

pred = s.predict_model(gbc)

# +
#pred['prediction_label']
# ...
# 695    1
# 451    0
# Name: prediction_label, Length: 154, dtype: int64

# +
# y_test
# -



metrics_binary(y_test, pred['prediction_label']).T

# ### object target

data = get_data('diabetes')



data['Class variable'] = np.where(data['Class variable']==1,
                                  "Positive",
                                  "Negative")

data.head()

X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(data.drop('Class variable', axis=1),
                                                    data['Class variable'],
                                                    test_size=0.2)
dat_train = pd.concat([X_train, y_train], axis=1)
dat_test = pd.concat([X_test, y_test], axis=1)

s2 = setup(dat_train, target = 'Class variable', 
      test_data = dat_test,
          session_id = 123)

gbc = s.create_model('gbc')

pred = s2.predict_model(gbc)

pd.crosstab(y_test, pred['prediction_label'])

metrics_binary(y_test, pred['prediction_label'], pos_label="Positive").T
```

### Issue Description

Hello PyCaret community, I will like to report an unexpected behavior from `predict_model()` when I want to do backtesting and forecast ahead prediction in future scenario simulated. I also want to take this opportunity to understand if what I'm doing here is correct.

The workflow that I will like to achieve is the following:

1. Initial month:  Train the best model, finalize it, and save the model as a pickle file.
2. Next month (future): I have a new data point. Load the saved model and update it with the new data point.

```python
from pycaret.datasets import get_data

### INITIAL MONTH ###

exp = TSForecastingExperiment()

# set up experiment without future data
target = 'Number of airline passengers'
exp = exp.setup(data=hist_data, target=target, fh=12, session_id=42, verbose=False)

# find best model
best_model = exp.compare_models(verbose=False)
final_model = exp.finalize_model(best_model)

# save the best model for use during future month
exp.save_model(model=final_model, model_name='final_model', verbose=False)


### FUTURE MONTH ###

new_exp = future_exp.setup(data=data, target=target, fh=12, session_id=42, verbose=False)

# load model that was saved during previous month
loaded_model = load_model(model_name='final_model', verbose=False)

# prepare new target and exogenous columns
new_y = new_data[[target]]
new_x = new_data.drop([target], axis=1)

# update model with new data
updated_model = loaded_model.update(y=new_y, X=new_x)

# trying to backtest

new_exp.predict_model(estimator=updated_model, verbose=False)
```

With a new experiment set up using dataframe consisting the latest data:

I don't get the same output you provide when running the examples. In number 3, I get Transformed data shape | (1460, 73), which is in line with expectations.

I would say all numbers are correct and in line with expectations. What you need to know is that `n_features_to_select=0.9` will take 90% of the starting features, not of the transformed features. If you want more, select an integer instead.

> Especially, in case of enabling the PCA nad feature_selection, I assumed that the targets values of feature_selection would be applied after PCA transformed.

Feature selection is applied after PCA, but indeed, the 0.9 is taken before the transformations, hence the error. If you rally want to use feature selection after PCA, and knowing `pca_components=5`, just select `n_features_to_select=4` or below 5 at least.

Ummm... In case of including the dummy encoding, does it work correctly?? I thought that it should be removed that category columns which selected by feature_selecte function from dataset. (i.e. some remain some of dummy columns in one categoly column??)
And I could not find the correct columns value after dummy... So, how should I know it to set the n_features_to_select in int value? In case of including the categoly, should I limit to use the float value for this parameters?

I reckon that it's not ideal to use an int when you don't know what the number of columns is going to be after the dummy transformation. Unfortunately, there is no better way. The reason the percentage is taken from the original dataset is because at runtime, we don't know how many columns will remain after all transformations before feature_selection.

You should not do `data=data`. `create_model` returns the estimator without the pipeline. If you provide the untransformed data to `predict_model`, it fails. You should do `predict_model(iforest, data=None)` to use the internal data, or provide the whole pipeline with new data.

```
dataset = pandas.read_csv('filename')
new_prediction = predict_model(saved_iforest, data=dataset)
```

```python
data = data[['date','internal_product_code']]
```

```python
from pydantic import v1 as pydantic_v1
```

Hi, first of all, thank you for providing us with such a wonderful library for automl tasks. I have been working specifically with `pycaret` Time Series module for a few weeks now. # customized a sliding window cross validation object

```python
    fh=np.arange(1, 12+1),
    window_length=48,
    step_length=10
)

# create a custom function

from pycaret.time_series import add_metric

def rmsle(y_true, y_pred):
    return mean_squared_log_error(y_true
                        , y_pred
                        , squared=False)

# feature engineering on target variable
from sktime.transformations.series.summarize import WindowSummarizer

kwargs_target = {
    'lag_feature':{
        'lag':[1,2,3],
        'mean':[[0,1],[0,2],[0,3]],
        'std':[[0,1],[0,2],[0,3]]
    }
}

]

expt = exp.setup(

  scale_exogenous='minmax',
  fe_target_rr=fe_target_rr,  # uncomment to disable feature engineering
  fe_exogenous=fe_exog,       # uncomment to disable feature engineering
```

km = s.create_model('kmeans')

### Issue Description

We have seen bug with logical error in FugueBackend  or TSForecastingExperiment implementation and need your assistance to debug this further

Running the below code with pip install numpy==1.22 fugue==0.7.3 pycaret==3.0.0rc4 cloudpickle prophet==1.1.4 lightgbm=3.3.5

1. I can reproduce the bug on DBR 14.0 (multiple node mode)
2. but the bug does not happen on DBR 14.0 (single node mode)

Note that for the same spark version, multiple node mode and single node mode have exactly the same execution environment, so that it can prove this issue is not caused by environment inconsistency.

and the issue seemingly is not related to python package versions, I install exactly the same python package versions for almost all python packages. 
Also it is unlikely to be spark UDF bug, because we have fully test for spark UDF

So I think the issue probably relates to logical error in code, i.e., for specific pyspark UDF inputs, the bug is triggered, because in different spark cluster mode,  the input spark dataframe might be partitioned / grouped in different row order / differnt spark task number, this causes the pyspark UDF might get different input data in these cases., and for some specific cases, the bug is triggered.

So I suggest can you add some printing command in pyspark UDF functions (they are defined in FugueBackend spark backend) for debugging purpose, and then you can check spark worker logs (from databricks cluster web portal) to debug it.

### pycaret version checks

- [X] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported [here](https://github.com/pycaret/pycaret/issues).

- [X] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://github.com/pycaret/pycaret/releases) of pycaret.

- [ ] I have confirmed this bug exists on the master branch of pycaret (pip install -U git+https://github.com/pycaret/pycaret.git@master).


### Issue Description

When using the predict_model() method with provided future exogenous data, 
the vast majority of the models do not use the future exogen data to make the prediction.

### Reproducible Example

```python
import pycaret.time_series as pts
import pandas as pd
from sktime.datasets import load_longley

longley_data = load_longley()[1].merge(load_longley()[0].rename("TOTEMP"), left_index=True, right_index=True)

experiment = pts.setup(data = longley_data.iloc[:-3], target = "TOTEMP", fh = 3, enforce_exogenous = True) #last 3 rows are used as future data

exogenous_models = list(experiment.models().index) #all models that should support exogenous data

future_data_exogenous = longley_data.iloc[-3:,:].drop("TOTEMP", axis = 1) #proper exogenous data
future_data_exogenous_0 = longley_data.iloc[-3:,:].drop("TOTEMP", axis = 1) #exogenous data with all values set to 0
for column in future_data_exogenous_0.columns:
    future_data_exogenous_0[column] = 0

for model in exogenous_models:
    try:
        best = experiment.compare_models(sort = "SMAPE", include = [model], cross_validation=True) 
        final = experiment.finalize_model(best)
        
        prediction_exogenous = experiment.predict_model(X = future_data_exogenous, estimator=final)
        prediction_exogenous_0 = experiment.predict_model(X = future_data_exogenous_0, estimator=final)

        print("Prediction with exogenous:",prediction_exogenous)
        print("Prediction with exogenous set to 0:",prediction_exogenous_0)
        print("Exogenous data has no impact:",prediction_exogenous.equals(prediction_exogenous_0))

    except:
        print("Model", model, "failed")
```


### Expected Behavior

Expect different outputs for the prediction when using future_data_exogenous and future_data_exogenous_0

### Actual Results

```python-traceback
In this case only xgboost gets different results and a lot of the other models fail.
I tried the same script with different datasets that i can not provide here, but everytime prophet was the only model where future data exogenous had an impact on the prediction.
```

<details>
3.0.0
</details>
I also tried it with version 3.0.4, same issue

body:
### Describe the feature you want to add to this project

`pycaret` is using specific parameter combinations for `sktime` based estimators that it ships with.

Optimally, these are already tested in `sktime` with the full modular test suite there, so no changes to `sktime` accidentally break the "favourite estimators" in `pycaret` downstream.

An example of this is found in [this issue](https://github.com/sktime/sktime/issues/4587#issuecomment-1546689788) where `AutoETS` was not tested with `auto=True` in `sktime`, but `pycaret` was relying on this setting. Also see https://github.com/pycaret/pycaret/issues/3523.

### Describe your proposed solution

The "recipe" to do this would be as follows:

1. for each pre-set of parameters in here https://github.com/pycaret/pycaret/blob/7f57794ed7d0ccc12750e45bace22afcbe9be622/pycaret/containers/models/time_series.py#L911, write down a small set of fixed parameter combinations that cover a good range of different values used in `pycaret`. The "desired property" is: if if breaks in `pycaret`, it should also break for one of those fixed parameter sets

2. find the respective estimator in `sktime`, and add these parameter combinations as returns of its `get_test_params` method. If the estimator does not have or inherit a `get_test_params`, it needs to be added according to the extension template (or follow the pattern from other estimtors of the same kind). Here's an example of such a PR: https://github.com/sktime/sktime/pull/4588, this was following the missing `auto=True` coverage in https://github.com/sktime/sktime/issues/4587.

3. the CI in the PR to the `sktime` repo will then automatically run the full test suite for those parameter combinations. If tests fail, either (a) report this as a bug on `sktime`, similar to [this issue](https://github.com/sktime/sktime/issues/4587#issuecomment-1546689788) and wait for an `sktime` dev to fix; or, (b) fix the bug yourself, in a second PR branching off the "added parameters" PR (an example would be https://github.com/sktime/sktime/pull/4589, branching off https://github.com/sktime/sktime/pull/4588)

### Describe alternatives you've considered, if relevant

Why is the setup() method calling pipeline.fit? This would be the first explanation for the performance drop. Secondly, if you set the n_jobs parameter greater that 1 in the setup, there's a lot of extract overhead as joblib is persisting large input arguments each time a pipeline step is called it seems. 

https://github.com/pycaret/pycaret/blob/ea88b2d3ee22c080ca5059f2f6f1547952b9451c/pycaret/classification/oop.py#L889C54-L889C54

> Why is the setup() method calling pipeline.fit?

`pipeline.fit` is called in order to get the data properties ending in `_transformed`, e.g. `dataset_transformed`. The fitted pipeline is later used in numerous methods, for example for plotting.

> if you set the n_jobs parameter greater that 1 in the setup, there's a lot of extract overhead as joblib is persisting large input arguments each time a pipeline step is called it seems.

I don't understand what the `n_jobs` parameter has to do with the caching of the pipeline steps you refer to (I think). If you are worried the caching is making it slow, set `memory=None` in setup and see what happens.

> > Why is the setup() method calling pipeline.fit?
> 
> `pipeline.fit` is called in order to get the data properties ending in `_transformed`, e.g. `dataset_transformed`. The fitted pipeline is later used in numerous methods, for example for plotting.
> 
> > if you set the n_jobs parameter greater that 1 in the setup, there's a lot of extract overhead as joblib is persisting large input arguments each time a pipeline step is called it seems.
> 
> I don't understand what the `n_jobs` parameter has to do with the caching of the pipeline steps you refer to (I think). If you are worried the caching is making it slow, set `memory=None` in setup and see what happens.

But that's exactly my point. The core issue is that there is a big change in behavior in `setup()` from 2.x and 3.0. Let's say I am _not_ performing any downstream plotting and just running `compare_models()` or 'tune_model` or something. The cached transformers are not (and should) not be used and I would have big concerns about data leakage if that were the case.

Look, the behavior change was forced onto the user without giving them an option to turn it off. I don't want you to run a full pipeline fit on my training data during setup. That just not good. Downstream, if I want to plot or perform other tasks, _then_, caching the transformers might make sense. For example, calling something like `plot_model()` or 'evaluate_model()` should cache the transformers upon first use then subsequent calls can use the `dataset_transformed`

When it comes to joblib, the logs are outputting the follow:
`UserWarning: Persisting input arguments took Xs to run. If this happens often in your code, it can cause performance problems (results will be correct in all cases). The reason for this is probably some large input arguments for a wrapped
function (e.g. large strings). THIS IS A JOBLIB ISSUE. If you can, kindly provide the joblib's team with an example so that they can fix the problem.`
The large input arguments are likely the `X_train` and `y_train` getting passed in. My point in calling that out was more of and FYI. Additionally since the default is `memory = True`, there is a lot of I/O overhead incurred while writing out those cached transforms.

Actually, in 2.x, the exact same behavior occured, _with the difference_ that the pipeline fitted in `setup()` was also used in model fitting - which indeed lead to data leakage. That has been fixed in 3.0, and the caching system has been introduced as a way to reduce the impact of recreating the pipeline for every model and every fold. The idea is that when you run `compare_models`, the first time each fold is visited, the pipeline will be cached and then reused for subsequent models (sans the model itself, of course). The joblib caching system we are using guarantees that the right cached objects are loaded given the arguments. However, you are correct that this introduces additional hashing and I/O overhead that in some cases may diminish benefits from caching. We will consider changing the default behavior to `memory=False`.
Keeping an eye on this but for large amounts of categorical columns

### Describe your proposed solution

The decision could be made based on several factors, including but not limited to the following

1. What does the roadmap of each of these versions of `sktime` look like and how does it align with pycaret's time series roadmap 
    - Time Series Clustering
        - Probably be one of the sktime versions, unless someone has opinions/facts that another lib would be better for this.  
    - Time Series Clasification
        - Probably be one of the sktime versions, unless someone has opinions/facts that another lib would be better for this. 
    - Time Series Anomaly Detection
        - ??  
    - Time Series Forecasting
        - Global Modeling
            - user global forecasting based on one of the sktime versions
            - `nixtla` backend for [global](https://github.com/Nixtla/mlforecast) modeling?
        - Hierarchical Forecasting
            - user hierarchical forecasting based on one of the sktime versions
            - `nixtla` backend for [hierarchical](https://github.com/Nixtla/hierarchicalforecast) modeling?
        - If going with `nixtla`
            - Current benchmarks make it faster than sktime (e.g. see [hierarchical comparison](https://github.com/Nixtla/hierarchicalforecast/tree/main/experiments/libs-comparison) and [Global modeling announcement](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/mergenthaler_machinelearning-timeseries-forecasting-activity-7033898837886816256-X4jI?utm_source=share&utm_medium=member_desktop))
            - How much of an additional effort would it be since we have a lot of code in common base classes? 
            - Would we need to have another variant of the base class for these "new" backend libraries?  
2. How does the roadmap of the two sktime versions impacts the existing time series forecasting functionality in pycaret and the support for it?
    - Time Series Forecasting
      - Time Series Feature Extraction (setup process)
      - Time Series Local Models 
4. What are the various time series tasks that are going to be supported in the two versions of sktime going forward?
5. Is there a critical mass of core developers to support and maintain each of these time series tasks in the two sktime versions.
    - Avoid single point of failures 
7. Timeline for the releases from the two versions of sktime?

**If anyone thinks of any other factors that should go into the decision, please feel free to comment below.**



### Describe alternatives you've considered, if relevant

The forked version of sktime was created from version 0.16.0 of the original sktime. Maybe for the time being, we pin sktime to 0.16.0 in pycaret until we make the decision above.

### Additional context

_No response_

comments.body: @skanjila FYI... If you have any thoughts, feel free to share them.

Another path could be that we support both the "original sktime repo" (called `sktime` as of this writing) and the "fork" (called `scikit-time`) as backend engines (now that we have this capability).

**Advantage**
- Takes the decision-making out of pycaret's hand and let's the user choose one of their liking (I personally like this since I don't wish to take sides in this dispute).

**Disadvantage**
- More maintenance is required from pycaret's developers. 
- Also changes are that something might break in the future (irreconcilable) if the 2 repositories diverge too much in terms of their backends (e.g. in the pipeline structure, etc.)

If we go with this path, we could even benchmark the 2 backends using [this library](https://github.com/pycaret/benchmarks), e.g how we do for Nixtla and sktime's implementation of [auto_arima and others](https://htmlpreview.github.io/?https://github.com/pycaret/benchmarks/blob/main/data/m3/M3_Monthly_smape_vs_time.html).

Anything else that anyone can think of?

Some answers to the above:

4. capacity/capability

on sktime "fork", it "looks like" there are a number of core developers, but if you check their GitHub history:

* none of them have been active in framework design, architecture. See commit/MR history and look at MR topics (base framework? general quality?)
* the majority of them don't have recent code contributions at all on sktime, or only punctual recent contributions, so their coding and maintenance capacity look inflated if you just look at numbers of "developers"
* the Tony Bagnall group especially has been a "single issue contributor group" around time series classification (and in there specific algorithms, not framework), yet they are very "loud" when it comes to shouting on governance related topics
* of course, you will observe in the next time inflated activity and posturing. To gauge actual capacity, look at the contribution logs over the last year.
* to gauge technical capacity, look at discussion threads like the one on numba https://github.com/sktime/sktime/issues/3567. It may make sense to a politician, but what about content?
* to gauge how they deal with communnity: the "fork" developers are prone to forming an aggressive mob, see, e.g., https://github.com/sktime/sktime/pull/2677, https://github.com/sktime/sktime/pull/3095, https://github.com/sktime/sktime/issues/3567 - from an ethical perspective, that shouldn't be encouraged. From a capacity/capability perspective, this has the effect of driving away contributors, and it creates mental pain just to look at it.

on sktime "original":

* contributors on "original" have been more silent more recently to avoid the heat, but are still there (see contribution log!). These are people who primarily want to code and participate in a friendly community, not people who like to shout in online discussions.
* we still have the full architectural capacity and maintenance capacity, including *all release managers*
* "driving away productive contributors" like in https://github.com/sktime/sktime/pull/2677, "ganging up" or other forms of adverserial behaviour are less likely to happen on the original project, now that those doing it are gone. It will, more likely, happen on the "fork"
* if you look at the history of the communtiy interaction channels (help desk on discord, contributors channel on the old slack), you see most helpful support replies coming from developers on the "original"
5. we'll keep releasing in 2-4 week cycles, aiming to support python 3.7-3.11. The fork have already broken deprecation patterns and does not seem like it will be downwards compatible.

1. key elements on the roadmap for `sktime` "original":

forecasting:

* enabling scale/distributed back-end `dask`
* forecasting & deep learning API and integrations
* probabilistic forecasting - backends
* speed-ups for hierarchical and global/reducer forecaster
* back-end integration work (e.g., `darts`, `nixtla`)
* graphical pipelines

framework:

* config interface like in `sktime`
* `skbase` base class refactor and separate package (this could also be adopted by `pycaret` for base interface homogeneization, you mention the base classes being back-end specific, etc)
* reducing & streamlining checks/conversions

time series classification, clustering, regression:

* distance choice is hard-coded and `numba` dependent. This will be made more flexible
* implementation/integration of more "standard" methods, e.g., `sklearn` classifiers for TSC that were missing
* better integration with `tslearn` package, joint API if possible
* alignment functionality - clean API

anomaly detection, annotation:

* base interface was not consolidated, base class API will be drawn up
* implementation/interfacing from backlog

2., 3.: for sktime original, none of the interface contracts will change in the forseeable future (2023, 2024), nor will the way how you construct pipelines, nor the set of supported tasks.

Note: the fork have already made hacky changes to base interfaces. This introduces breakage risk. Example: in forecasting, the internal format of the `cutoff`, was changed back to time stamp from `pd.Index`. This will lose the support for `freq` by `pandas` and run off a deprecation cliff at some point.

see point above, related to architecture, design, release management
This is already causing issues with installation; for the time being, it can be fixed if python is fixed at >= 3.9, < 3.14. But it might stop working in the future...

body:
### Describe the feature you want to add to this project

Upon an un expected kernel interruption, for example a memory issue or server failure, the optimization pipeline (ensembling, tuning, blending) seemingly cannot be continued. 

Scenario:
• Create setup and save config
`save_config('config_file_name')`
• Compare all models and save top 5
`top_5_models = compare_models(n_select=5)` + foreach `save_model(top_5_models[i], 'path/to/file')`
• Begin optimization pipeline (e.g. tuning)
`tuned_model = tune_model(top_5_models[0])`
--KERNEL FAILURE--

At this point, if I'd to start tuning top_5_models[0], there seems to be no way.

### Describe your proposed solution

One solution would be to have a modified load_model with an additional flag that would allow (in combination with load_config) resuming the optimization pipeline from wherever it was left off. For instance, if the step was a tuning, or an ensembling, all models gotten from compare_models or create_model would be available for tuning or ensembling.

### Describe alternatives you've considered, if relevant

I've tried loading a trained model either from its initial training out of `compare_models` or `create_model` with loading the config that was used prior to training (e.g. `load_config`) to no avail.

### Additional context

This feature request assumes that throughout the training process, all steps/models/configs are saved to disk. For example, if a model was just ensembled with `ensembled_model = ensemble_model(model_to_ensemble)`, right after that line is processed, `save_model(ensembled_model, 'path/to/file')` is called such that if it were desired to use ensembled_model later down the pipeline (e.g. blending models) it could be done.
title: Ability to Continue the Optimization (Tuning, Blending, Ensembling) Pipeline Upon Unexpected Kernel Interruption

Hi @ngupta23, 

I was looking into this, and initially, I thought the `_set_fold_generator` function in the [oop.py](https://github.com/pycaret/pycaret/blob/97649adf8965fd02831c14982a48323b6ce7de4c/pycaret/time_series/forecasting/oop.py#L967) file under time_series/forecasting directory was not handling fold number calculation properly:

```python
def _set_fold_generator(self) -> "TSForecastingExperiment":
    """Sets up the cross-validation fold generator for the training dataset."""
    possible_time_series_fold_strategies = ["expanding", "sliding", "rolling"]

    if not (
        self.fold_strategy in possible_time_series_fold_strategies
        or is_sklearn_cv_generator(self.fold_strategy)
    ):
        raise TypeError(
            "fold_strategy parameter must be either a sktime compatible CV generator "
            f"object or one of '{', '.join(possible_time_series_fold_strategies)}'."
        )

    if self.fold_strategy in possible_time_series_fold_strategies:
        # Number of folds
        self.fold_param = self.fold
        self.fold_generator = self.get_fold_generator(fold=self.fold_param)
    else:
        self.fold_generator = self.fold_strategy
        self.fold_param = self.fold_generator.get_n_splits(y=self.y_train)

    return self
```

So, I modified the second if block to calculate the fold count for CV objects like `ExpandingWindowSplitter` correctly:

```python
    if self.fold_strategy in possible_time_series_fold_strategies:
        # Calculate the fold_param based on splits
        self.fold_generator = self.get_fold_generator(fold=self.fold)
        self.fold_param = (
            self.fold_generator.get_n_splits(y=self.y_train)
            if hasattr(self.fold_generator, 'get_n_splits') else None  
        )
```

This fixed the output. So running the same code as you, I got this:  
  
![image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/e68ce85d-db42-45ef-873c-a407af001578)

Now the fold number is showing up correctly. I was about to make a pull request with the changes I have made, however, at this point, I started looking at the documentation of [Pycaret's Time Series libraries](https://pycaret.readthedocs.io/en/latest/api/time_series.html#pycaret.time_series.TSForecastingExperiment). And I found out that the `fold` parameter should only get `int` type argument, and the CV objects should be passed to the `fold_strategy` object instead!   

So, your code should be modified to this: 
```python
# !pip install pycaret==3.0.0rc3

import numpy as np
from pycaret.time_series import TSForecastingExperiment
from pycaret.datasets import get_data
from sktime.forecasting.model_selection import ExpandingWindowSplitter

y = get_data(114, folder="time_series/seasonal", verbose=False)
cv = ExpandingWindowSplitter(fh=np.arange(1, 13), initial_window=24, step_length=4)
exp = TSForecastingExperiment()
exp.setup(y, fh=12, fold_strategy=cv)
```
This should return the output as expected!

However, since passing a CV object to the `fold` parameter still runs the code without throwing an error and returning the object as the `Fold Number` in output, I believe we should raise a TypeError when any type of argument except `int` is passed into the `fold` parameter. So I have modified the `setup()` function in `pycaret/time_series/forecasting/oop.py` and inserted the following code block: 

```python
# Validate fold
        if not isinstance(fold, int):
            raise TypeError(
                f"The 'fold' parameter must be an integer. You provided: {type(fold).__name__}. "
                "If you intended to use a custom cross-validation object such as SlidingWindowSplitter or "
                "ExpandingWindowSplitter, please pass it to the 'fold_strategy' parameter instead. "
                "The 'fold' parameter is ignored when 'fold_strategy' is a custom CV object."
            )
```

I am making a pull request. Let me know if you have any suggestions!

### pycaret version checks

- [X] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported [here](https://github.com/pycaret/pycaret/issues).

- [X] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://github.com/pycaret/pycaret/releases) of pycaret.

- [X] I have confirmed this bug exists on the master branch of pycaret (pip install -U git+https://github.com/pycaret/pycaret.git@master).


### Issue Description

Since the creation of the first codebase of version 3 of pycaret still under development, scikit-learn as well as other non-scikit-learn package models, such as lightgbm, xgboost, catboost, have been updated to newer versions, for example scikit-learn now at version 1.1.2, and since then there have been many updates. So I think the parameter list should be checked for the models that pycaret uses, as well as the parameters for tune_model. I believe that pycaret can exploit the new parameters of the models, otherwise the models will only work in default mode.

What I propose is a checklist to check if you are using all the current parameters of the most recent versions of the models.

- scikit-learn - All params checked for latest version?
- catboost -  All params checked for latest version?
- lightgbm - All params checked for latest version?
- xgboost - All params checked for latest version?

I think the file to check is pycaret\containers\models\classification.py for example to update classification parameters code.

**UPDATE (2022-09-27):**
- CatBoost is now in version 1.1. All params should be checked according to new version.
- Other idea is comment the code with something like "Date:xxxx-xx-xx - Checked for version: x.x"


### Reproducible Example

```python
.
```


### Expected Behavior

tune_model to explore all possible parameters to extract best possible results

### Actual Results

```python-traceback
.
```

### Describe the feature you want to add to this project

The Anomaly library within pycaret contains many useful methods for anomaly detection. However, as with PyOd and other outlier detection libraries it is up to the user to set the amount of contamination that exists in the dataset as an input parameter. This parameter is often difficult to ascertain and is where PyThresh comes in. PyThresh is a library for taking outlier detection scores and thresholding these scores to provide a threshold between inliers and outliers with many available statistical methods. The methods provided by this library follow a similar structure to PyOd and are a quick add on the already existing decision scores calculated after fitting an outlier detection method. More info can be found on https://github.com/KulikDM/pythresh. 

### Describe your proposed solution

PyThresh would be a great addition to pycaret's anomaly library as it simplifies the need for thresholding decision scores generated by outlier detection methods. It is not limited to only PyOd methods, and is a straightforward addition to the already existing format.

### Describe the feature you want to add to this project

For risk assessment models, calibration of the predicted probabilities is as important as having good discrimination between classes. When using CalibrationClassifierCV, with a base estimator that has already been fitted, the calibration should be done on a separate dataset (calibration set) from the training to avoid overfitting. At the moment, PyCaret offers only a two-dataset split (Train, Test) defined in the setup function either through a split or by explicit declaration.  

### Describe your proposed solution

As Antoni Baum kindly suggested, that may be accomplished by combining the train and calibration data before the setup function and setting as a CV splitter with correct indices using the predefined split (https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.model_selection.PredefinedSplit.html#sklearn.model_selection.PredefinedSplit)

Suppose that you have three data frames (df_train, df_cal and df_test)


#Initially, you merge the train and calibration sets.

from sklearn.model_selection import PredefinedSplit
df = df_train.append(df_cal)

#Then define the input data for all three; GroundTruth is your target variable

X_train = df_train.drop('GroundTruth', axis=1)
X_cal = df_cal.drop('GroundTruth', axis=1)
X_test = df_test.drop('GroundTruth', axis=1)

#And then define the indices and the PredefinedSplit
train_val_idxs = np.append(np.full(X_train.shape[0], -1), np.full(X_cal.shape[0], 0))
ps = PredefinedSplit(train_val_idxs)
result = next(ps.split(df), None)

and in the setup function, you pass fold_strategy=ps

After completion of the setup function, and to get access to X_train, X_cal and X_test, you run the following code:

X_train_old = get_config('X_train')
Y_train_old = get_config('y_train')
X_test = get_config('X_test')
Y_test = get_config('y_test')

X_train = X_train_old.iloc[result[0]]
Y_train = Y_train_old.iloc[result[0]]
X_cal =  X_train_old.iloc[result[1]]
Y_cal =  Y_train_old.iloc[result[1]]

body:
### Describe the feature you want to add to this project

Today I spent some time responding to posts on the issues page and found that most problems with installing pycaret are due to systems with python 3.7.

From what I've seen some problems reported are not even from pycaret but from other packages that have been updated and do not correctly support python 3.7, consequently leading to pycaret reporting errors that do not belong to it.

So, to avoid problems and "force" people to upgrade to more up-to-date systems, I think pycaret should have python 3.8 as a minimum requirement.

This will avoid most problems with unrelated packages and thus avoid reporting problems on the pycaret issues page.

Also, I think it doesn't make sense to use python 3.7 anymore, because most people use Jupyter Lab and newer packages of jupyter lab give problems with python 3.7.

### Describe your proposed solution

Python 3.8 as minimum requirement

### Describe alternatives you've considered, if relevant

_No response_

### Additional context

If pycaret team not agree with that, pycaret should create warnings about that.

Packages like jupyter-lab, should show warnings for those using python 3.7.
I think this is an example: https://github.com/pycaret/pycaret/issues/2825

However i found more one problem: Google Colab uses Python 3.7.... Can we encourage Google Colab to update to Python 3.8...

Any ideas?

comments.body: We discussed this but decided not to drop support for Python 3.7 yet because colab still uses 3.7 as default version, and a lot of our users rely on colab. Nevertheless, we will drop it sooner rather than later.

I think we have a thorn in the side because with python 3.7 we can only have scikit-learn 1.0.2 which has a lot of problems and consequently these problems will bring more problems for pycaret even if the pycaret code is correct.

The minimal version of scikit-learn that pycaret should be 1.1.2 recently released which has many bugfixes and has minimal python 3.8 support.

In my opinion something should be done to abandon python 3.7.

Can anyone talk to Google Colab and know when they will switch to Python 3.8?

Another very strong argument is that pycaret is based on scikit-learn, that is, if pycaret uses a lot of scikit-learn functions, then it should use a highly updated version, without errors or problems, so I insist that we should switch to python 3.8 to at least use scikit-learn 1.1.x

More:
- Scikit-Learn 1.0.x have not updates since 6 Apr 2022, you can see here https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/commits/1.0.X

@tvdboom we can also make a manual to install python 3.8 on google colab (https://stackoverflow.com/questions/60775160/install-python-3-8-kernel-in-google-colaboratory) and so our problem is solved. I want to know your opinion about that

> @tvdboom we can also make a manual to install python 3.8 on google colab (https://stackoverflow.com/questions/60775160/install-python-3-8-kernel-in-google-colaboratory) and so our problem is solved. I want to know your opinion about that

Installing a custom version of Python on colab is "hacky" and prone to get many errors. I wouldn't recommend doing that.

> Can anyone talk to Google Colab and know when they will switch to Python 3.8?

It's a well known issue on their github (see https://github.com/googlecolab/colabtools/issues/2165 for example). It's unclear when/if it's going to happen.

> Another very strong argument is that pycaret is based on scikit-learn, that is, if pycaret uses a lot of scikit-learn functions, then it should use a highly updated version, without errors or problems, so I insist that we should switch to python 3.8 to at least use scikit-learn 1.1.x

This is a less bigger problem than you might think since Python 3.8+ users can use the latest version of sklearn. They are not restricted to older versions (only when you use Python 3.7). The only hiccup here is that our code base needs to be backward compatible until sklearn version 1.0.2

title: [ENH]: Make minimum python version >= 3.8

### Describe the feature you want to add to this project

When running the `.check_stats()` method, the current available tests are:

Test | Name
---|---
Summary | Statistics
White Noise | Ljung-Box
Stationarity | ADF
Stationarity | KPSS
Normality | Shapiro

I would like to add other tests to this list of options. Including:

Test | Name
---|---
Seasonality | [QS](https://rdrr.io/cran/seastests/man/qs.html)
Seasonality | [Seasonal Strength](https://pkg.robjhyndman.com/tsfeatures/articles/tsfeatures.html#stl_features)
Regularity | [Regularity](https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/zoo/versions/1.8-8/topics/is.regular)
Stability | [Stability](https://pkg.robjhyndman.com/tsfeatures/reference/lumpiness.html)
Stability | [Lumpiness](https://pkg.robjhyndman.com/tsfeatures/reference/lumpiness.html)
Auto-Correlation | [ACF](https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/stats/versions/3.6.2/topics/acf)
Auto-Correlation | [PACF](https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/stats/versions/3.6.2/topics/acf)

The URL is given for where to find more information about these specific tests.

### Describe your proposed solution

Some of these tests are already implemented in the [`statsmodels`](https://www.statsmodels.org/) library. Such as the [`acf()`](https://www.statsmodels.org/dev/generated/statsmodels.tsa.stattools.acf.html#statsmodels.tsa.stattools.acf) and [`pacf()`](https://www.statsmodels.org/dev/generated/statsmodels.tsa.stattools.pacf.html#statsmodels.tsa.stattools.pacf) functions.

However, some of the other ones are not yet written in Python. They are, however, implemented in `R`. Such as the [`qs()`](https://rdrr.io/cran/seastests/man/qs.html), [`is.regular()`](https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/zoo/versions/1.8-8/topics/is.regular), [`stability()`](https://pkg.robjhyndman.com/tsfeatures/reference/lumpiness.html), and  [`lumpiness()`](https://pkg.robjhyndman.com/tsfeatures/reference/lumpiness.html) functions.

So, in the same way that PyCaret has implemented the [`_is_gaussian()`](https://github.com/pycaret/pycaret/blob/time_series_beta/pycaret/internal/tests/stats.py#L81) function, I propose to craft some similar functions to handle the above tests.

I am planning to add Cumulative Forecast Error (CFE), which is the summation of error at each period (Actual - Forecast). The negative value of CFE will represent over-forecast, whereas the positive value will represent under-forecast.

It can also help us track how the bias is changing with forecast horizon (whether it is degrading or remaining stable).

When you do this, pay special attention to the cases where fh has gaps. for example, fh = [2, 3, 4, 10, 11, 12] should only divide CFE by 6 (since there are 6 data points in the FH) and not 12.

You may also need to add unit tests to check for these conditions. Some examples of how this is done for other "custom" metrics can be found here.
