**Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.**

In time series, many libraries provide the same models. Example, 

AutoARIMA is available from pmdarima and a faster variant is available through statsforecast that now has a plugin in sktime.
Similarly, there are plans to probably add AutoARIMA from statsforecast to darts as well.

```python
from sktime.forecasting.arima import AutoARIMA  # from pmdarima
from sktime.forecasting.statsforecast import AutoARIMA  # from statsforecast
```

**Describe the solution you'd like**

Provide a way for users to choose the engine they would like to use for the model. One example could be 

```python
create_model("auto_arima", aggregator="sktime", engine="pmdarima")
create_model("auto_arima", aggregator="sktime", engine="statsforecast")
```

In the future if darts is available as a plugin in sktime, we could do something like this

```python
create_model("auto_arima", aggregator="darts", engine="pmdarima")
create_model("auto_arima", aggregator="darts", engine="statsforecast")
```

**NOTE: The aggregator has to be available as a sktime extention for this to work.**

**Additional context**
This is similar to the engine concept in [R/tidymodels](https://www.tidymodels.org/start/models/#new-engine), although we are separating the aggregator from the 

> However, now that the type of model has been specified, a method for fitting or training the model can be stated using the engine. The engine value is often a mash-up of the software that can be used to fit or train the model as well as the estimation method. For example, to use ordinary least squares, we can set the engine to be lm

comments.body: @moezali1 @Yard1 here are my thoughts about this topic. Feedback is welcome.
This sounds good, though I would be leaning towards making that a setup option.

I was thinking that we will have a default priority list of aggregators and engines. But users will be able to provide their own priority to override that. The default list of engine priorities would be stored in the model container itself. The default list of aggregator priorities would be an input to `setup` and possibly overwritten in `compare_models` through a user accepted argument.

I will draft the interface for review.

@moezali1 @Yard1 @FedericoGarza PR has been submitted for implementing this without the aggregator (since we only have sktime for now)

# Usage

## Global settings (using setup)

```python
from sktime.forecasting.arima import AutoARIMA as PmdAutoARIMA
from sktime.forecasting.statsforecast import StatsForecastAutoARIMA

#### Set engine globally ----
exp.setup(data=data, engines={"auto_arima": "statsforecast"})

#### Produces a statsforecast model ----
model = exp.create_model("auto_arima")
assert isinstance(model, StatsForecastAutoARIMA)

exp.compare_models(include=["auto_arima"])
assert isinstance(model, StatsForecastAutoARIMA)
```

## Local Changes

```python
#### default auto_arima engine is pmdarima for now ----
exp.setup(data=data)

#### Produces a pmdarima model ----
model = exp.create_model("auto_arima")
assert isinstance(model, PmdAutoARIMA)

#### Override model engine locally ----
model = exp.create_model("auto_arima", engine="statsforecast")
assert isinstance(model, StatsForecastAutoARIMA)
# Original engine should remain the same (since the above changes was local to the call only)
assert exp.get_engine("auto_arima") == "pmdarima"
model = exp.create_model("auto_arima")
assert isinstance(model, PmdAutoARIMA)

# You can repeat the same for compare_models as well
```

## Notes;
1. Currently `statsforecast` is an optional library. Once we have thoroughly vetted functionality in pycaret, we can make it a required dependency and switch this to be the default for `auto_arima`.
2. For some reason, on the airline dataset, `pmdarima` produces better results than `statsforecast` and also takes less time. More vetting is needed. The time issue can be tracked here: https://github.com/Nixtla/statsforecast/issues/177
3. There seems to be an issue in `statsforecast` when uninstalled, so we can potentially see issues with the optional dependency checks in `pycaret` and `sktime`. See https://github.com/Nixtla/statsforecast/issues/118

body:
**Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.**
Users do not have a convenient way to plot ACF and PACF on the seasonal component of a time series decomposition. 

**Describe the solution you'd like**
Allow the ability to run ACF and PACF on the seasonal components of decomposition. This will allow for users to determine the P and Q values to be used for modeling ARIMA.

Refer to Konrad's 2nd Time Series notebook (see link below)

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/33585645/156904842-7e528330-1f6f-4afb-9d7b-61bbfe04bff3.png)


**Describe alternatives you've considered**
Fetch the decomposition data from the plot, then create a separate experiment with the seasonal component and plot ACF and PACF for this.

```python
from pycaret.datasets import get_data
series = get_data("airline")

exp = TSForecastingExperiment()
exp.setup(data = series, fh=12, fig_kwargs=global_plot_settings, session_id=42)
decompositon = exp.plot_model(plot="decomp", data_kwargs={"type": "multiplicative"}, return_data=True)

eda = TSForecastingExperiment()
eda.setup(data = decompositon.get("seasonal"), fh=12, fig_kwargs=global_plot_settings, session_id=42)

eda.check_stats(test="adf")
eda.plot_model(plot="pacf", data_kwargs={"nlags": 12})
eda.plot_model(plot="acf", data_kwargs={"nlags": 12})
```

**Additional context**
- [ ] Add link to Konrad's notebook here.

body:
**Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.**
I'm currently working on a supervised machine learning project, where the type of problem is regression. I have detected some outliers (based on my target variable) in the EDA part, and even though I have read that big outliers will affect the MSE of my model, I wanted to still keep them in my modelling part.

I wanted to know whether those outliers are influential observations, and exactly know which of those outliers change the parameters of my fitted models, and be able to identify and specifically analyze those points. I have read that with Cook's distance, these data points can be detected, and it is one of the plots that are available in `plot_model()`. 

However, I'm not able to see which exact data points are influential, the x-axis plots the indexes, but with many datapoints, it is impossible to detect the specific indexes.


**Describe the solution you'd like**

I would like to receive those indexes in array, or if possible, a dataframe with the influential observations.

**Describe alternatives you've considered**

I have seen in the code that for the Cook's distance plot, the following import is made [`from yellowbrick.regressor import CooksDistance`](https://www.scikit-yb.org/en/latest/api/regressor/influence.html),  and tracing it to `internal/plots/yellowbrick.py` where the actual graph is generated and plotted. 

Maybe will it be possible to then access visualizer attributes, and using the `visualizer` attributes after (yellowbrick.py - line 87):
```python
elif handle_train == "fit":
        logger.info("Fitting Model")
        visualizer.fit(X_train, y_train, **fit_kwargs_and_kwargs)
```
and from those attributes return a dataframe with influence points? 
Not sure if by using the attributes `distance_`, `p_values_` and `influence_threshold_`, we could use the indexes and return the specific datapoints that are higher than threshold?

**Additional context**
Add any other context or screenshots about the feature request here.

Hi @ngupta23 just to clarify that I have that step to only make sure non-negative values are not fed into models that cannot handle that. I personally prefer having the "full" predictions and manually clipping these later according to the domain. Reason is unclipped predictions are more symmetric and represent model uncertainty better, whereas clipping can "fool" downstream users if that makes sense.
Anw commenting here as curious to follow the implementation.

@ngupta23 I feel that both implementations have their use cases. Might be useful to have an upper limit, lower limit and 'clamp method' parameters. If the user simply wants to clamp predictions they could do this themselves but the implementation suggests we want to fit/evaluate the forecasters based on user-defined clamps

> just to clarify that I have that step to only make sure non-negative values are not fed into models that cannot handle that. I personally prefer having the "full" predictions and manually clipping these later according to the domain. 

@atsangarides @AJarman Thinking about this more, the use case in this issue is actually slightly different form what @atsangarides describes. Here we are saying that the data (naturally) does not exceed the limits. For example, energy consumption is always positive (> 0). So the training data will always be positive. But if the trend is decreasing, future predictions (or intervals) may be negative. The use case in this issue is just limiting the future predictions to be clamped to 0 for example by providing a lower clamp level.  

The use case that @atsangarides presents has negative values in the data itself. So it is a different use case. I don't think that is what we intend to support here.

> Reason is unclipped predictions are more symmetric and represent model uncertainty better, whereas clipping can "fool" downstream users if that makes sense.

This is true for the use case that you describe. For the one that is being addressed here, clamping probaby makes sense since metrics will get computed based on clamped values (0 in the example above) instead of negative values which is probably more representative.

Thoughts are welcome.

> If the user simply wants to clamp predictions they could do this themselves but the implementation suggests we want to fit/evaluate the forecasters based on user-defined clamps

@AJarman By the way, the way @ltsaprounis has implemented the transformer, if the training data itself is outside the limits specified by the user, the transformation will fail since the premise is that the training data is within the limits naturally and we are just trying to clamp the predictions to be within the same limits. @ltsaprounis - correct me if I am wrong.

I am actually dealing with energy demand/price forecasting :) 
I started clamping my predictions when they were actually made, but moving away from that, and handling clamping differently in different places.
If you use forecasts as inputs to an optimiser, you can use lower/upper quantiles for including uncertainty. Even though you cannot have <0 values for say demand, clipping your predictions could impact how you penalise different markets. All I am saying is that depending on what a user wants to use the forecasts for, clipping at an earlier stage might not be desirable. No  right or wrong answer 😄

@atsangarides - Got it. In any case, the way this will be implemented, user will be in control. They can decide to clamp the predictions or just leave it as is (default). So this would address both cases :)

**Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.**
Chaining of methods is generally easier to read compared to nested functions.

```python
# Nested functions
best_dt = ensemble_model(tune_model(create_model('dt'), choose_better=True), choose_better=True)
```

**Describe the solution you'd like**

Chaining of methods in OOP API. Example [here](https://www.linkedin.com/feed/update/urn:li:activity:6854113630401675264?commentUrn=urn%3Ali%3Acomment%3A%28activity%3A6854113630401675264%2C6854296751881486336%29&replyUrn=urn%3Ali%3Acomment%3A%28activity%3A6854113630401675264%2C6854738909985853441%29)

```python
best_model = (
    experiment
    .create_model('lr')
    .tune_model(choose_better=True)
    .ensemble_model(choose_better=True)
)
```

**Additional context**

- We could provide an argument in setup called `enable_chaining = True` that will switch from returning the models to returning the experiment object which will enable the chaining.
- Also, internally, we will have to store the results from all steps so that they can be referenced in the next step.

body:
Threshold optimization can be very important to maximize cost for a given model (https://pycaret.org/optimize-threshold/).

I am facing a situation where all my data rows have true/false-negative/positive costs proportional to some features in the database.
For example, my true positives cost would be **a** \times db['cost'], and my false positive cost would be **b** \times db['cost'].

I do not think that Pycaret allows this feature, but it would be, in my opinion, a good idea to allow functions as arguments for more permissivity.

I could suggest something like   
def f(row):
   return **a** \times row['cost']
def g(row):
   return **b** \times row['cost'] 
    
And then do a as following: 
optimize_threshold(xgboost, true_negative = f, false_negative =g, use_function = True)

The temporary alternative is to code this functionality by hand,  or to assume that mean(true_negative) is similar to mean(false_negative); in this case, the cost maximization can still be trusted
title: feature dependant threshold optimization

body:
Following my reply on LinkedIn to @moezali1 call for new features, here is a big one

**Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.**
Since #573 it has been possible to fit models with `sample_weights` argument. However sample_weights are consequently ignored in pycaret metrics, evaluation and are not used to split the data at `setup` stage.

**Describe the solution you'd like**
I propose, as originally suggested in https://github.com/pycaret/pycaret/issues/573#issuecomment-684041587, to implement a `sample_weight` argument in the `setup` function which would be _automagically_ used:
- to split the data into train/validation/test (currently NOT in scikit learn, see https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/issues/4632#issuecomment-393945555 for possible implementation)
- as an argument to fit, possibly removing all the scikit learn regressors/classifiers that do not support `sample_weights` by default in `compare_models`
- as an argument to all metrics, note that, for classification problem scikit-learn `auc` doesn't have a sample weight argument, so you'll need a whole new AUC definiton, similar to the one in [this example in the scikit-learn documentation](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/auto_examples/linear_model/plot_poisson_regression_non_normal_loss.html#evaluation-of-the-ranking-power)
- in the model evaluation graphs (this probably at a later stage and in a future issue, since is much less urgent that the others)

**Describe alternatives you've considered**
I did try to create my own metrics with `add_metric` and using train data from `get_config`, but I messed it up badly (I think beacuse of internal cross val splits). I don't see proper `sample_weights` implementation as something doable _on top of_ pycaret without proper implementation _in_ pycaret.

**Additional context**
`Sample_weights` argument is key in most insurance/credit risk modeling problems, known under the name of _exposure_ particularly when modeling frequency of losses, which typically is representable by a poisson process. The assumption that underlies the poisson process is that the probabilty to observe an event is proportional to the time of the observation. Length of the contract, i.e. the previously mentioned _exposure_ is thus fundamental when modeling. A good example of practical use of `sample_weight` (with metrics using `sample_weight`, but with no validation split) is available in the [scikit learn documentation](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/auto_examples/linear_model/plot_poisson_regression_non_normal_loss.html#sphx-glr-auto-examples-linear-model-plot-poisson-regression-non-normal-loss-py)


The PyCaret training process yields a data preparation pipeline and a model. They can be manually combined into an `PMMLPipeline` object and then converted to PMML representation using the [SkLearn2PMML](https://github.com/jpmml/sklearn2pmml) package as usual.

Example:
```python
from pycaret.regression import *

# Do the standard PyCaret stuff

from pycaret.regression import prep_pipe
from sklearn2pmml.pipeline import PMMLPipeline

pmml_pipeline = PMMLPipeline([
	("prep_pipe", prep_pipe),
	("final_model", final_model)
])

from sklearn2pmml import sklearn2pmml

sklearn2pmml(pmml_pipeline, "regression.pmml")
```

@vruusmann I have recently refactor `save_model` function to append estimator as a last step of pipeline so that only one object i.e. `Pipeline`  is saved as `pkl`, where last item of the pipeline is a trained `estimator`. (see `/pycaret/classification.py` on master). What I am trying to do now is add a parameter `type` in `save_model` so that when somebody selects `pmml` as type the entire `Pipeline` which is a combination of `prep_pipe` and `estimator` and stored in a parameter called `model_` is converted as `pmml` and saved on local disk. However I realized in doing so I am getting an error from `sklearn2pmml` due to `prep_pipe` object. (see error above). I also tried to just save estimator instead of the entire pipeline (this is not ideal though). At estimator level, I am having issues with these estimators in `classification.py`:

- lr 
- gpc
- lda 
- qda,
- ada,
- catboost

I am planning to add this feature in `2.1` (targetting release by end of Aug 2020). 

Are you able to help?

> Exception in thread "main" java.lang.IllegalArgumentException: The object (Python class numpy.core.multiarray._reconstruct) is not a PMMLPipeline

The SkLearn2PMML package saves the `PMMLPipeline` object to a temporary file in Pickle data format, and then executes a Java command-line application to perform the conversion work.

The above exception means that the Java application is looking into the pickle file, but cannot find the `PMMLPipeline` object in it. Instead, there's an unexpected `numpy.ndarray` object.

TBH, I got this exception myself, when making the above comment: https://github.com/pycaret/pycaret/issues/345#issuecomment-668748620

It appears to be the case that PyCaret is meddling with the definition of `joblib.dump` function, so that the `PMMLPipeline` object somehow gets replaced with the `numpy.array` object. I've never seen this "object replacement" happen before, so I kind of blame PyCaret here (overriding the `joblib.dump` using globals somehow?).

The workaround is to save the `PMMLPipeline` object manually, using the `pickle.dump` function:

```python
pmml_pipeline = PMMLPipeline([
	("prep_pipe", prep_pipe),
	("final_model", final_model)
])

import pickle

with open("regression.pkl", "wb") as pf:
	pickle.dump(pmml_pipeline, pf)
```

And then execute the [JPMML-SkLearn](https://github.com/jpmml/jpmml-sklearn) command-line application manually on the `regression.pkl` file.

> How do we load back pmml pipeline in notebook?

There is no going back from PMML to a (ML framework native-) Python object. PMML documents can be evaluated using PMML engines, such as [JPMML-Evaluator](https://github.com/jpmml/jpmml-evaluator) for Java or [JPMML-Evaluator-Python](https://github.com/jpmml/jpmml-evaluator-python) for Python.

> I have recently refactor save_model function to append estimator as a last step of pipeline so that only one object i.e. Pipeline is saved as pkl

I looked into `save_model` functions about a week ago when I was trying to figure out how to fetch all the pieces (ie. `prep_pipe` and `final_model`). Sure, replacing an array `[prep_pipe, final_model]` with a single pipeline object is a step in the right direction.

Perhaps you should introduce a PyCaret-specific `Pipeline` subclass, at least for persistence (save/load) purposes? A custom pipeline class would make it possible to store all sorts of metadata in there (target transformations etc), plus make it easier for third parties to establish the identity of the pipeline object. For example, if the pickle file contains class `pycaret.pipeline.PyCaretPipeline`, then it would be fairly easy to associate it with the PyCaret framework.

 > I am trying to do now is add a parameter type in save_model...

PMML is a one way street. The save operation translates low- to medium-level PyCaret/Scikit-Learn/Python representation (binary, machine-oriented) to a high-level PMML representation (text-based, human-oriented).

Perhaps you should keep `save_model`/`load_model` functions unchanged, and if necessary, introduce a separate `export_model` function? For starters, perhaps it will be sufficient if PyCaret documentation simply states that some PyCaret pipelines can be translated to different representations using different tools (plus examples)?

> At estimator level, I am having issues with these estimators in classification.py

Some Scikit-Learn estimator to PMML converters have not been built yet, and some only work for limited configurations.

The PMML export functionality should come with a "limited support" disclaimer ("limited export functionality, dependent on a third-party package").

For starters, the SkLearn2PMML package first needs to learn about custom PyCaret transformation classes (eg `DataTypes_Auto_infer`), so let's not rush it.

after trying for a while I've come to the same conclusion, however, saving the model only works without a problem except when it comes to `LogisticRegression`, one must explicitly specify the `multi_class` argument to either `ovr` or `multinomial`, this is possible in pycaret==2.0 so
```
lr = create_model('lr', multi_class='ovr')
save_model(lr, format="pmml", model_only=True) 
```
this code works, but I don't think it would be of great use.
